key_insight: Oncology-specific language models performed best when they were either further pretrained on local notes or built with a bespoke oncology tokenizer, showing that both adaptation and tokenization matter.
clinical_relevance: For NLP systems used on real outpatient oncology notes, domain-specific model design may improve term handling, masking predictions, and representation quality compared with general biomedical encoders.
method: Trained and compared RadBERT, PathologyBERT, OncoNote-RadBERT, and OncoNoteBERT on 290,026 UK outpatient oncology notes from 21,564 patients.
Evaluated models with masked language modeling loss, perplexity, tokenizer fragmentation, clinical term tokenization, masked-token probes, and representation analysis.
Compared zero-shot external encoders with continued pretraining and training-from-scratch strategies.
evidence_signal: OncoNote-RadBERT had the best corpus fit (perplexity 2.10), while OncoNoteBERT had the most efficient tokenization and correctly handled 12 of 13 masked-token probes versus 7 of 13 for OncoNote-RadBERT.
watch_item: Better perplexity did not always mean better clinical token prediction, so tokenizer fragmentation and local validation should be checked before deployment.
paper_title: OncoNoteBERT: A Foundation Representation Model for Natural Language Processing of Real-World Outpatient Oncology Notes
